sledy-na-vode: Traces on the Water is a novel by Roman Surzhikov, the first book set in a new fantasy world the author himself calls the “World of Wells.” It takes place in three countries where steam engines, revolvers, slavery, and wells that grant miracles coexist. The book opens with a preface in the voice of the writer Alvaro da Silva, then shifts to third-person narration and alternates between three storylines: Alvaro in Catalia , the slave Red in a Dangarian forest, and Lieutenant Dietrich in Dangar and Ollandia . The protagonists do not meet, but their fates are connected by people they have in common and by the wells themselves. Title The exact phrase “traces on the water” does not occur in the novel: a search across all chapters finds no instance, and the book offers no explanation of its title. The only direct indication comes from the author. In January 2026, a viewer of his livestream asked whether Alvaro was writing a book called Traces on the Water, and the author confirmed that this was exactly the book Alvaro was writing. The novel thus becomes a “book within a book”: the writer-protagonist creates the text we read. The livestream host called this device a “book within a book”;
alvaro-da-silva: Alvaro Flores da Silva is a writer from Laerta , one of the three main characters of Traces on the Water and the only one who introduces himself to the reader: he writes the preface in the first person before switching to the third. He earns his living from novels, gives lectures to aspiring writers, and dreams of a gold bracelet and a place beside his grandfather on the Great Scroll . His storyline is an investigation: to write the commissioned book about the heroes of the Solantan Expedition , he begins looking into the strange death of one of them and gradually finds himself at the center of events far more dangerous than literary arguments. Origins and family (ch. 0–13) Flores is the name of a family “rich in poets, writers, and playwrights.” Of the entire family, only Alvaro’s grandfather, Ricardo Flores , produced a masterpiece: his novel The Snake in the Reeds brought its author fame and wealth, and his name was inscribed on the Scroll. Alvaro’s father, Ricardo’s son, “was lost in his father’s radiance” and spent his life as an obscure playwright at a minor theater; he received his maestro’s bracelet late in life, a year before alcoholism ruined him. amir-sedoj: Amir the Grey is the magnus, head of the order and guild of fishermen, the fischmeisters . Dietrich calls him the third man in Dangar and the most mysterious of the world’s rulers. He appears in person in only one scene in the novel, but is discussed in other chapters as well. Appearance and manner The Grey dresses in the fashion of high society, but his frock coat is azure with golden stars, resembling a wizard’s robe from a fairy tale. He has gray hair, a long, narrow beard, and woolen gloves: the old man’s hands get cold. He speaks smoothly, in a “voice of sea waves,” which calms his listeners. Joriksen addresses him as “Your Wisdom” and “mentor.” Joriksen’s teacher (ch. 21–23) Otto, the secretary, tells Dietrich that Joriksen is the finest fisherman of his generation and a pupil of Magnus Amir the Grey, but not yet an oberfischmeister. In chapter 23, Baron von Landau , the oberfischmeister of Dunkwald, tells the hunter Yakka that everyone serves someone: the Grey serves the Sower and the great truth, while the baron himself serves the magnus and the guild. balboa: Don Balboa owns an arms factory in Laerta and is one of the manufacturers of the esfera of Production. The reader knows of him only through other people's accounts: he does not appear in any scenes, but his decisions set the events of ch. 11 in motion. The Obreros' Riot (ch. 11) According to Lucille , two days earlier obreros dismissed because of steam-powered machines, backed by bankers from the esfera of Finance, challenged the factory-owning dons to a debate in the Chamber of the Word . The manufacturers did not attend, sending lawyers from the esfera of Law instead; the friends believe they were directed by Fatima-allen . The obreros lost the debate, went to Balboa's arms factory, and were beaten there by guards and Shadow's thugs. Newspapers repeated the factory's account of “madmen with torches,” which outraged the esferas of Craft and Service. The narrator observes that Balboa himself had already miscalculated: had he honestly admitted ordering the dismissed workers to be beaten, he would have been called cruel, but it would not have caused a sensation. beatris: Beatriz , more often called Golden Quill in the novel, is an Academy of Arts student who attends Alvaro da Silva’s literature lectures. To him, she is initially an irritating star pupil in the front row, then a companion, driver, and investigative assistant. Unlike the heroes of the books Alvaro writes on commission for Don Filippe , Beatriz has not yet completed a single book of her own. According to the author, she is a bright, straight-A student who knows the theory but has yet to write anything in practice. Character and appearance Beatriz is red-haired, confident, and bold; Alvaro considers her presumptuous. She is methodical: every morning she records the previous day’s important events in her diary and carries a notebook and pencil. She reads widely, enjoys technical details, and understands them better than one might expect of a writer: in ch. 9, she presents General Deserey with a theory that artillery strength increases with the square of the number of shots, and he agrees. Beatriz’s passion is speed. boroda-lopatoj: “Spadebeard” is the nickname Red gives one of the Foreman’s four subordinates. The novel does not give his real name. The dugout (ch. 8) Every evening he returns from work with clumps torn out of his beard and smooths over the bare patches. In ch. 8, when Red breaks up the gang, Spadebeard receives a blow to the Adam’s apple. Ch. 15–19 In ch. 15, he meets Red at the spring with Hoarse and stares at him, unable to believe he is alive. In ch. 19, Baron Landau shows Red his pit: Spadebeard does not have to dig with his bare hands; instead, he plucks a hair from his beard and puts it in each shovelful of earth. Red even feels relieved: one could live with a Zustand like that.
brigadir: In the novel, “foreman” is a position rather than a name: it is the title of the senior slave in a dugout. One such man is depicted in detail—the foreman of the dugout to which Red is assigned in ch. 4. Other foremen are mentioned only in passing. The Position and Other Foremen In the slave settlement, each dugout is run by a foreman. He occupies the best bunk beside the stove, receives a triple portion, assigns duties, and controls the distribution of food, but does not work as his subordinates do. A foreman remains a slave and “Guild property,” as the sentence in ch. 12 emphasizes. Foremen are mentioned in the plural in ch. 27, when the baron sends not only soldiers but also “trusted” slaves, foremen, and scribes to search for the fugitive. In ch. 15, Red is given a separate dugout, and the scribes register him as a “foreman” (in the sense of the holder of the dwelling and its ration). This is merely an entry in the ledger: he has no subordinates. The Foreman of Red's Dugout (ch. 4–8) In ch. 4, he is a ruddy, shaven brute trying on the boots taken from Red; Red strikes him in the face with his heel. brojenshtoff: Brojenstoff is a Dangarian general of infantry, one of the three commanders of the armies that invaded Ollandia . He appears in person only once in the novel, at a conference with Field Marshal Reiniger ; on other occasions, the Catalians discuss him. The Conference in Latsen (ch. 31) The senior officers of the Ollandian theater sit around a green table at the field marshal's headquarters in Latsen : the “lean” Lieutenant General Hofmeyer , two “fleshy” generals of infantry— Kurtzleben and Brojenstoff—and Reiniger himself. The field marshal calls on Brojenstoff to report first. After the capture of Latsen, the three armies went their separate ways: Brojenstoff led his into the northern “shepherd” provinces, Kurtzleben went south toward Bargot , and Hofmeyer went east toward Mershants . The narrator calls Brojenstoff the least capable of the three commanders, while noting that little had been expected of him in the first place. Northern Ollandia is mountainous, and the Dangarian infantry of stones is weak in the mountains. dezerej: Gabriel Deserey is a general in the Catalian army and third on the list of heroes whom Prim-Allen Filippe di Berro commissions Alvaro da Silva to describe. He took part in the Solantan Expedition , but he stands out in the novel for another reason: he is the character most concerned by the threat of war with Dangar and prepared to demonstrate it with figures. This anxiety drives him in his scenes with Alvaro and Fatima . Character and appearance Deserey is polite and warm, yet somewhat detached. He speaks of his children and subordinates with warmth, but as though from a distance. He takes literature seriously: he admires Alvaro’s prose, but criticizes the fighting in his novels with professional severity. He keeps diaries and promises to give them to the writer. Meeting at Ortiyar (ch. 9) Deserey invites Alvaro by letter to an inspection at Ortiyar fortress, thirty miles from Laerta . The writer arrives with Fernan Gereira and Beatriz . diego-ingres: Diego Ingres is the alguacil at the Foucault Street station whom Alvaro approaches after finding a woman’s severed finger at home. Alguacils and guards (ch. 13) The narrator explains that two bodies maintain order in Catalia ( Alguacils ): guards from the esfera of Shadow — bearded, without mustaches, and with red scarves on their heads — intervene in obvious crimes, while alguacils from the esfera of Law — with pointed beards and a white feather of the mirna Iolanta in their hats — determine the extent to which the Scroll has been violated. Ingres is an alguacil. He loves his work; his habits include saying “hmm-hmm” when interested and tilting his head to the left when he hears nonsense. On the white land of the Arts district, there are no straightforward crimes: neither murders nor thefts. Instead, creative people devise situations in which it is difficult to tell whether any crime has occurred at all. Ingres relates two anecdotes, one about a composer who burned someone else’s cantata, the other about a singer and her poet neighbor. ditrikh: Dietrich von Dort is an artillery lieutenant in the Dangarian army, an “eagle” nobleman without land or slaves. He is one of the three main characters of Traces on the Water; his storyline concerns a man who once saw the future in a well, used it in war, and has been paying for that step ever since. His story begins in chapter 2 and passes through occupied Ollandia, Dangar’s capital Hofstadt , and back to Ollandia. According to the author, the characters’ storylines are offset in time and will “come together in a particular way”; Dietrich’s story takes place later than Red’s (see the interview section for more). Character and appearance Dietrich’s middle name is Wolfgang, also the first name of Major von Klein , but the novel does not indicate any connection behind the coincidence. The novel’s first description of Dietrich takes the form of a letter: Staff Captain Claus von Zeidvist describes his twenty-three-year-old subordinate to the colonel. A graduate of the Kaiser Ferdinand II Artillery Academy, he is strong in mathematics and ballistics, an unremarkable-looking, gentle man: short, with a bulbous nose, a small chin, and a slight paunch. elza: Elsa von Walbrecht is a baroness and owner of the Beautiful Well, one of Hofstadt’s schönbruns. Her mansion on the Wunde is styled after a steamship. She hosts an annual fishing party “for select society,” is a friend of Master Fritjof Joriksen , and knows how to smooth over any conflict at her table. The house and the well (ch. 14–21) The mansion stands in northern Hofstadt between the docks and the railway bridge. It has three stories, granite columns shaped like steamship funnels, windows resembling cabins, and a paddle wheel turning in the pond to the right of the entrance. The novel explains that the house was built here because the schönbrun is here; the palace is merely a handsome accessory. The well is hidden in a round, white pavilion with stained-glass windows, resembling a conservatory. Dense parkland surrounds it, liveried guards carry double-barreled guns, and girls in glasses stand watch at the entrance. Inside the pavilion is a small theater with velvet chairs, where spectators look down into the well through mirrors on the ceiling. emil: Emil Diale is Doctor Juanes’s butler: an imperturbable man who hides his bracelets beneath his sleeve and drags one leg. He appears twice in the novel, and on both occasions it is his account that advances the investigation. The first visit (ch. 5) He meets Alvaro and Fernan at the house on the edge of the Valentian Gardens and shows them into the study. Emil says that the doctor was a very good man and describes his last day: visitors, tea, nausea toward evening, and a climb onto the roof. He argues with the widow over who should tell the story and shows the cabinet containing patients’ gifts, including a bottle of ten-year-old Almagarian bonk from the last visitor. To reassure Alvaro, he says that he tried the bonk himself on the day of the funeral and found no poison. During the visit, in his own words, he “could not fail to notice the white land.” Exposure (ch. 24) When Alvaro returns with Beatriz , Emil tries to keep them out. The writer reconstructs the day of the death. Left alone in the study, Emil poured some bonk into an empty vial to take away: a glass would have retained the smell. farmiga: Don Farmiga is dean of the Faculty of Letters at the Academy of Arts, where Alvaro lectures on literature. Refusing an advance (ch. 3) After a lecture, Alvaro tries to obtain an advance from the dean for several future classes. Farmiga reminds him that the last time the lecturer received money, he disappeared for two weeks and owed the academy five classes. He threatens that if Alvaro continues disappearing, his lectures will be given instead by Cecilia Armani, Olesia’s finest female poet, who has moved to Laerta. Demanding an outline (ch. 13) In ch. 13, Farmiga writes Alvaro a letter demanding that he urgently send an outline of his forthcoming lectures. Fernan puts the letter on the desk with the rest of the unread mail.
fatima: Fatima Ir-Reya is prim-allen of the esfera of Law, one of the lawyers’ three representatives at the High Table . At first she is heard about through others: obreros call her a “serpent” and “Iolanta’s merciless sword,” her associates wear bracelets with a black snake, and she herself rarely appears in court, directing her pupils from the shadows. To Alvaro , she is one of the five heroes of the Solantan Expedition whom Don Filippe asks him to write about, and the one he fears most: the lawyers of Law whom she leads have long symbolized the law’s cold power. The novel repeatedly compares her to the mirna Iolanta , patron of law. Character and position Fatima heads an esfera whose craft is debate. Her pupils, the “little serpents,” enter the Chamber of the Word with a single task: to win. Even one who is not among her best, Vincente Ramires , easily defeated Alvaro in his first debate. Her detractors call her the “judicial cobra” and “serpent.” According to Fernan, she does not personally address juries but oversees important cases. fernan-gerejra: Fernan Gereira is Alvaro da Silva's loyal friend, a street scribe, and a committed reformist. Because of his place in the social hierarchy, he constantly reminds the protagonist of the world's injustices; together with his wife Lucille , he represents the “ordinary person's” view of Catalia that Alvaro argues with in almost every chapter. In the investigation, he is first a skeptic, then a secretary and scribe, and finally a participant in the fight at the castle. Character and Occupation Fernan works as a scribe: he writes down the words of illiterate obreros and composes messages for postcards, greetings, and love letters. His speech is florid and grandiloquent. Work is becoming scarcer as people learn to read and write, and he must live on modest earnings of about a hundred escudos a month. He is a man of culture, avoids fights, and makes no secret of his fear: when Carlos el Niña points an unloaded pistol at him, Fernan faints. At the same time, he is stubborn and stands firmly by his views: he regards the rich as “parasites” and “bloodsuckers,” and occasionally calls Alvaro a long-eared ass. filippe: Filippe di Berro is an opera singer and prim-allen of the esfera of Art, one of the rulers of the High Table . He commissions Alvaro da Silva to write a book about the heroes of the Solantan Expedition , setting the novel’s main action in motion. He himself is not on the list of heroes: he calls the expedition’s participants his friends, but the novel says nothing about any role of his own in the voyage. Character and appearance According to the narrator, Filippe is known for his vindictiveness and his tendency to cause scenes. He has kept his seat at the High Table for six consecutive years, although the Table expels the worst of its allens every year, by using theater, books, epigrams, and caricatures against his political enemies. Offstage he looks like an aging, puffy-faced gentleman with yellow patches on his face; onstage he wears a corset. A Muari servant in a white tailcoat with scarlet buttons accompanies him. Filippe is polite and ironic, but sharp when necessary: he can lower his voice an octave and speak harshly. flammel: Flammel is an oberfischmeister of the Fishermen’s Guild. He does not appear in person in the novel: Magnus Amir the Grey and Fritjof Joriksen speak about him. Investigation (ch. 29) The Grey assigned Flammel to investigate the destruction of Dunkwald . He recently interrogated Joriksen and prepared a report that the magnus read “with a smile on his lips”: it reveals that the master is hiding something. The Grey knows Joriksen lied to Flammel and says the master apparently has his own grievances against the oberfischmeisters: despite his talents, Joriksen is still not one of them. Joriksen's Assessment (ch. 31) Describing the interrogations to Major Klein , Joriksen says Flammel does not fully understand his own power, which made him easy to deal with. The Grey proved truly dangerous. The novel does not reveal how Flammel's investigation ended.
frafra: Franz Freiber, also known as Fra-Fra, is a fair-haired young man whom Dietrich encounters in queues for appointments at the capital's government offices. He appears in one scene in Chapter 10. Conversation in a Beer Hall (ch. 10) Dietrich is looking for a position in Hofstadt, visiting office after office and being turned away everywhere: his temporary discharge and interrogation by the Kaiser’s Claws have barred his way into the army, so he is trying to enter the civil service. The fair-haired young man, whom he has seen in queues more than once, takes him to a beer hall and explains the rules: do not bother without a recommendation; the queue is only for show, and the position goes to someone who has a word put in for him; recommendations must be sought from people of standing—a governor, councilor, judge, or administrator. When Dietrich replies that he has no influential acquaintances, the young man introduces himself: Franz Freiber, or simply Fra-Fra. He knows the lieutenant's name and offers him a temporary position that, he claims, is sheer pleasure rather than work. frej: Frey is the woman who drives Fatima Ir-Reya’s black steam carriage and guards her employer. She barely speaks in the novel, but appears armed at the moments when she is needed. The stranger’s chauffeur (ch. 24–28) In ch. 24, during his meeting with the stranger, Alvaro notices a gloomy female chauffeur with hair cut short “like a boy’s,” contemptuously smoking a pipe while he escapes the anatomical theater. She is named only in ch. 28: Alvaro calls her “the sullen creature who drives your car,” and Fatima corrects him: this is Frey, and “there have been recorded occasions when Frey smiled.” Fatima’s housekeeper and companion is named Yasmina. Last Winter (ch. 34) In ch. 34, Frey enters the castle cellar first, moving with an experienced gunfighter’s gliding gait, instantly assesses the situation, and holds the wounded killer at gunpoint. A wisp of smoke rises from her revolver’s barrel; when Beatriz says they managed without help, she replies that they “certainly did.” Fatima explains that she came to Tres Molinos incognito with only Frey: two bored ladies inspected the castle, took Javier Salam’s tour, and found a rusty component in the castle. gelb: Gelb is a noncommissioned officer commanding a fusilier platoon composed almost entirely of stones. He is coarse and faultfinding: during Dietrich’s inspection, he shouts at a soldier for a stain on his uniform and promises ten lashes, until the lieutenant cancels the punishment. He knows his men: he calls the holy-fool stone Salvation and considers Killnot, who cannot kill, the platoon’s “most valuable soldier.” The night of the escape (ch. 2–6) In the morning, Dietrich finds Gelb in a hut: he has been nailed to the wall through his palms and feet, and his jaw is smashed. He is badly wounded but alive. Dietrich orders Salvation to remove the nails and bandage his wounds, but runs off himself at the sound of horses. By the end of the battle, Gelb is dead. Dietrich gives Major Klein a different account, claiming that he tried to carry the wounded man, while Klein suggests that Gelb was abandoned to die. Escape (ch. 33) In ch. 33, the rifleman Killnot from his platoon is revealed to be Red . Gelb himself does not appear in this chapter.
gizeke: Frau Gieseke owns the house in Hofstadt’s Widows’ District where Dietrich von Dort’s family rents an apartment. She is the third generation of widows in her family: her mother and grandmother were also widows, and she traces her ancestry to the first widows for whom Empress Augusta ordered narrow three-story houses built within sight of the palace instead of granting allowances. Character The narrator calls her an exception among landladies: family honor prevents her from descending to landladies’ favorite occupation, quarreling with tenants. She does not spy on them or find fault with trifles such as an unlocked door. At the same time, she is too fond of mentioning death and seems to flaunt her close acquaintance with it, which unsettles Dietrich. She is convinced that Mari will soon be widowed, so she calls little Heinz “the little orphan” and readily helps Mari with water or cloth for diapers. She loves Dietrich like a son and is old enough to be his mother. Role in the story (ch. 10–25) In ch. 10, she meets Dietrich on the stairs with tears of joy, serves him and his orderly Milosh tea and schnapps, and gives Milosh a bench in the servants’ room. greta: Greta is a slave from the women's hamlet attached to the Dunkwald camp, where Red digs a well. She first appears as a “prize” for completing a well, then becomes his lover and the only person to visit him regularly in the pit. Her fate is one of the book's most harrowing storylines. Character and Appearance Greta is rosy-cheeked and healthy, with a black braid and a high bosom; Red first sees her in an embroidered shift. She does not know Catalian and is initially frightened of her visitor. It later emerges that she is deeply devout: she believes in the Sower as Red has always believed in himself, and considers everything in life, including slavery, to be God's will. She loves fine clothes and ribbons, weeps with joy on visiting town for the first time in years, and fears breaking the law to the very end. Her trade in the camp is to be a “prize” for slaves rewarded for their work. The other stones hate her because she has “bought her way out with other work” and does not dig the pit. Red sees a blue swallow on her door: every woman in the hamlet has a different picture on hers. izabel: Isabel is Carlos el Niña's wife. When first seen at the fort in the Old Port , she seems a fragile, sickly woman whom her husband protects like a little bird. By the middle of the novel, she disappears; it later emerges that nothing was as her husband or the reader believed. Appearance and Character Isabel is thin and nervous, with a long neck bearing a large mole and eyes of unequal size: the left is larger than the right. She speaks softly, her phrases trailing off into ellipses. The novel does not name her illness: for many years she was tormented by an affliction that made her “wither like a flower without water.” She reads Alvaro da Silva's novels. Her laugh rings out clearly; according to Carlos, she once had the loveliest laugh of all the girls in Laerta. At the Fort (ch. 7) Carlos tells his guests how they met on the day of the running of the bulls along Del Toro Boulevard: Isabel stood on the terrace of the Eliste Gallery , and he, hoping to win her heart, ran with the bulls and escaped them at the cost of his trousers. Everyone laughed except her. She was the one who guessed that the buried well in the fort's cellar was special and insisted it be dug out. Seeing a wilting
joriksen: Fritjof Joriksen is a Dangarian fischmeister , a master fisherman known to the reader through two of the novel's storylines. In Red's storyline, he is the young head of the Dangarian camp at Dunkwald, where slaves are forced to dig wells in the hope of producing a schönbrun ; in Dietrich's storyline, he is already a first-rank master, accepting expensive commissions from the owners of Wells. In an interview, the author named him as one of the Dangarians he likes. Character and Appearance Joriksen has sharp cheekbones, a hawkish nose, and green eyes; in Dunkwald, he wears a purple cloak with a silver catfish-shaped brooch and a black square cap, while in the capital he wears a white cloak and a gold-trimmed tricorne, with a foreign naval uniform full of pockets beneath the cloak. The master is energetic, proud, and irritable when his plans go awry. His favorite sayings are “money is dust” and “a schönbrun is no shop, and I am no merchant.” He speaks like a trader, yet sincerely believes in the subject of his craft and in the people on whom he stakes his hopes. kajzer: The Kaiser is Dangar’s ruler. He does not appear as a character in Traces on the Water, but is constantly invoked: people fight, serve, and arrange marriages for his sake. The novel does not give the sovereign’s name; the characters know him as “the Kaiser,” “the emperor,” or “His Majesty.” What is known about the ruler (ch. 2–33) Power and the army. Regulations prescribe the response to a greeting: “By the great Kaiser’s victory! Our service is our pride!” Officers regard their duty to the Kaiser as paramount, and Dietrich speaks to Major Klein of duty to the Kaiser and the fatherland. The special division known as the Kaiser’s Claws obeys orders only from Schlissel and calls itself the sword in the Kaiser’s hand. Preferences. According to Count Lurd , the emperor likes meek, modest people and has a weakness for artillery. In matters of dynastic marriage, he usually trusts Lurd’s own analysis. Information. He reads Count Wahrheit’s Glory of the Empire, and in chapter 14 the baroness relates that the Kaiser doubted her word but agreed once he heard that Glory had reported the matter. Three powers. karlos: Carlos el Niña is a pirate-smuggler, a don of the esfera of Shadow , and the owner of a former fort in the Old Port of Laerta . He appears first on the list of heroes for the book commissioned from the writer Alvaro da Silva by Prim-Allen Filippe di Berro : a “buccaneer,” a participant in the Solantan Expedition . To Alvaro, he is a man easily made into a hero, but Carlos himself dreams of something else: being known as the book's villain. Character and Appearance Carlos wears a black captain's outfit with gold epaulettes and a hat with three scarlet feathers; a double-barreled pistol and a dirk are tucked into his belt. He is boisterous and fond of theatrical gestures; he attended the premiere of the opera Senorita Violet and borrowed his pistol “joke” from it. His main affliction in peacetime is boredom. He keeps his men under strict discipline; Alvaro considers him an honest man, although he remembers that Carlos once shot a captain who had done wrong. Carlos treats his wife with conspicuous tenderness: he calls her his “little bird,” orders a shawl and tea with honey for her, and forbids “gloomy talk”—discussion of deaths—in her presence. karmensita-estevos: Carmensita Estevos is an obrero of the esfera of Shadow, a woman from a harbor brothel, and mother of Rodrigo da Vira’s son. She does not appear in person in the novel. Information about her comes from two sources: Alvaro da Silva finds her in the records of the Great Scroll , while Red, in Dangarian captivity, remembers the mother of his son — Kara. Kara and Carmensita The novel does not explicitly state that they are the same woman, but everything fits. Red is da Vira, as revealed in ch. 34. Kara is an “obrero of Shadow, a girl in your trade”; Carmensita is an obrero of the esfera of Shadow from a harbor brothel. Both bore a son to the same man, and the son remained in Laerta. Prim-Allen Filippe di Berro adds his name to the list with a black eyebrow pencil, saying that he died the day before yesterday and is indifferent to fame. The mystery of his death is the first that Alvaro solves. lid-anteodor: Lid Anteodor is a hero of Catalian tales, a great knight whose victory over the hosts of the Muari ruler Faid-Musa is known throughout the country. He is present in the novel only in conversations and songs: his name exemplifies the scale of a victory in Alvaro’s debate with Ramires and he is the beloved hero of legends that Red knows and sings. His image in legend (ch. 15) Catalians consider Anteodor their own in a very real sense: each of Catalia’s five lands claims to be the knight’s birthplace. There are therefore a great many stories about him — at least five complete sets and numerous smaller variants. The novel says nothing about his origins or biography beyond these tales. As Red recounts them, the tales of Anteodor combine the buoyant optimism of stories about the mirnas with stern lessons about the power of the Ancients . Hidalgo Lid is brave but not stubborn, decisive but not blind. He charges into battle when necessary, but also knows how to reach an agreement when words can settle the matter. To achieve his aim, he is ready to use cunning, guile, and even seduction; in a hopeless situation, he can retreat to save himself and his warriors. Mention in the debate (ch. 1)

The book and the philosopher’s own story run through the novel’s middle third: it inspires an exhibition at the Eliste Gallery , attracts Alvaro da Silva’s attention, and ultimately leads him to the castle above Tres Molinos . Philosophy and reputation Van Halm was born in Mergana ; his surname speaks for itself, but he spoke Catalian fluently. About twenty years earlier, the Academy of Sciences invited him to Laerta. He wrote that horror is a step beyond the edge of the ordered world into chaos, and that all development is such a step. The book and the exhibition’s paintings feature the “Lords of the Abyss” (see Ancients ): Ai-Khinar, the Shipbreaker, and Mother-and-Father. The bookseller Jose Flarbo tells Alvaro that ahead of him in sales are the memoirs of Colonel el Cameda, who died in a duel, and van Halm’s book. Flarbo’s account (ch. 16) The philosopher lived and wrote on an old estate in Selezia , until he sent away the servants and locked himself in. She appears only in Dietrich’s scenes, always in connection with money and domestic peace. She runs the household firmly, repeatedly scolding and correcting the stone maid, and expects her husband to respect her rules at home. Dietrich regards her character with respect and fear. He believes there is more will and life in his wife’s little finger than in all of Princess Olkha , which is precisely why her weakness, when it appears on one occasion, throws him off balance. The man “talked and talked, always about the same thing.” Red would have killed him if it had not meant smelling a rotting corpse for weeks afterward. rajniger: Field Marshal Reiniger is the highest Dangarian commander in the Ollandian theater. In chapter 31, he holds a conference in the former assembly hall of the Latsen voivodeship’s nobility, now his headquarters, and announces changes to the campaign plan. The conference in Latsen (ch. 31) Reiniger sits at the head of the table, gloomy as a storm cloud. Beside him are Lieutenant General Hofmeyer and Generals of Infantry Kurtzleben and Brojenstoff . Reiniger listens to reports, but has already made his decision: the meeting’s purpose is to communicate new orders to his subordinates. Brojenstoff is to continue distracting the northerners in the mountains; he does not need to capture large territories. Kurtzleben is given sixty days to force a crossing of the Khursla and besiege Bargot , but without a frontal assault: to avoid unacceptable casualties, four divisions from Hofmeyer’s army will make a flanking movement through the river’s upper reaches. Hofmeyer is left with half his army and is merely to maintain the siege of Mershants . When he proposes an assault across the frozen marsh by two or three hundred eagle cavalrymen, the field marshal rejects it as suicidal and orders him to di
red: Red is a Catalian whom the reader first meets in Chapter Four: bound, without boots, and thrown from a cart into a forest slave camp on the edge of Dangar. The author explicitly calls him the novel's third main protagonist, alongside the writer Alvaro da Silva and the Dangarian officer Dietrich von Dort . His storyline tells of a slave forced to dig a well and shows Dangar at its darkest: according to the author, Red's position in Dangar is comparable to that of a concentration-camp prisoner. Character and Appearance Red is tall—taller than all his dugout companions—broad-shouldered, and dark-haired. He is quick-tempered, cannot stand baseness, stupidity, or worthlessness, and fights better than anyone he has encountered: he handles a shovel so skillfully that he can scatter four men in a minute. He says he believes in three things—intelligence, his fists, and the mirna Eliga —“in precisely that order”; he also invokes the Ancients and the First Judge . Eliga, the mirna of luck, is also depicted on his forearm: a beauty sitting on a cannon, with two faces, one woman's and one snake's. At first, Red knows no Dangarian, although he speaks Muari and Solantan, neither of which helps he
rikardo-flores: Ricardo Flores is Alvaro da Silva's grandfather on the Flores side of the family. In the novel, he is present only through his grandson's stories. Alvaro describes the Flores family as rich in poets, writers, and playwrights, and his grandfather as its only member to have created a literary masterpiece and inscribed his name on the Great Scroll . Alvaro himself is firmly determined to become the second. The Snake in the Reeds Ricardo's major work is the novel The Snake in the Reeds, which his grandson calls a jewel of world literature. Alvaro calls his grandfather Don Ricardo and says he died basking in fame and wealth. Family (ch. 13) In ch. 13, while explaining to the guard Salvador at Don Maduro's how people become dons in Catalia—through skill, not inheritance—Alvaro talks about his family. His father, Ricardo's son, was overshadowed by his own father's brilliance: afraid of failing to live up to him, he spent his entire life as an obscure playwright at a small theater. He never dreamed of the title of don.
salvador: Salvador is a mercenary in the guard of the manufacturer Maduro . For much of the novel, he remains a nameless threat; his name is revealed during the interrogation at the mansion. Interrogation at Maduro’s (ch. 11–13) In ch. 11, when the train carrying machines for Don Balboa is stopped, Alvaro strikes the hired thugs with the butt of his revolver during the fight; the account in ch. 11 says that one is hit in the nose. In ch. 13, a man with a broken nose sits at a table in the guardroom of Maduro’s mansion: his name is Salvador, and he says that he fought on Balboa’s side. He interrogates Alvaro, accuses the Reformists of sabotage, and demands to know their aims. Not knowing them, the writer sets out his own program and leaves with his hand on his revolver: detaining someone on white land is a crime. The attack and threats (ch. 18–34) The attacker in the Old Port — tall, with a hoarse voice — shoots through Alvaro’s palm in ch. 18 after ordering him not to write. His name is not given then; only in ch. 34 does Alvaro recognize the voice in the courtyard of Last Winter castle and address Salvador by name, reminding him that he ordered him to abandon the book and spared him in the
shpeer: Speer is a lieutenant commanding the battery’s first platoon. When Zeidvist dies, Dietrich takes command and Speer silently obeys (ch. 2). Role in the battle (ch. 2–6) Formally, Speer should have replaced the commander. In ch. 6, Dietrich explains to Major Klein that he acted as he did because Speer comes from the hares while he is an eagle, and the soldiers would be more likely to trust an eagle. Dietrich adds that Speer afterward admitted he had been right. After the battle, Speer and the gun-crew commanders attend to the wounded and prisoners. He is not mentioned again in the novel.
shults: Schultz is one of the Foreman’s four subordinates in the dugout where Red is placed in ch. 4. Red can barely distinguish Dangarian names and remembers only the red-haired fellow with the split eyebrow. Ch. 4–8 Schultz is the first to dare object when the Foreman orders Red beaten. He receives the worst bunk, beside the entrance. In ch. 8, red-haired Schultz, his feet frostbitten, passes Red his supper and huddles beside the stove. After the morning beating, Red knocks him unconscious against the stove. Frostbite (ch. 12) When Red’s well reaches its seventh yard, Schultz suffers frostbite in his right foot, and his toes are amputated. He struggles with fever for three days and receives no food: by law, only those who work are fed. Red fills a bowl himself, but Schultz refuses out of fear, pulls a felt boot over the bloodied dressing, and returns to his Zustand on the fourth day. The digger (ch. 19) In ch. 19, Baron Landau shows Red the camp: Schultz digs his pit naked below the waist, with no toes on one foot and rotting toes on the other. Red doubts that he will live until spring, but Schultz continues digging.
siplyj: Hoarse is the nickname Red gives one of the four slaves in his first dugout: by evening, his voice gives out and he mutters prayers. His real name is not stated in the novel. The Dugout (ch. 8–12) In ch. 8, when Red breaks the work gang's resistance, Hoarse drops to his knees of his own accord, crying, “Nein! Bitte, nein!” He then sits down to eat at the common table. In ch. 12, he is the one who explains to Red through gestures that the foreman withheld food not arbitrarily but according to the law: only those who work are fed, and he should not be angry about the lashes. After the Escape (ch. 15) When Red lives separately, Hoarse and Spadebeard encounter him at the spring and “goggle at him as if he were a winged toad.” Later, he comes with the foreman to Red's dugout to look for a noose mark and leaves empty-handed.
spasenie: Salvation is a stone soldier in NCO Gelb's platoon. As the NCO explains, he received his nickname for his answer to the question of how the war would end: instead of reciting the regulations, he says salvation will come and God will save everyone. The others see him as a simpleton. Faith and Character (ch. 2) During Dietrich von Dort's inspection, he smiles joyfully, certain that God will save everyone “to the very last,” even the officers and the field marshal, but not the enemy: good people, yes; enemies, no. Dietrich envies the ease with which he has made peace with his conscience. At the well in the cellar on the hill, Salvation turns the winch, repeating that their salvation lies in the dear water. He condemns his escaped comrades: he says there will be no salvation for them. Escape and Killing (ch. 2) The platoon escapes at night, while Salvation, who refused to go, is left tied up in the hut beside Gelb, who has been nailed to the wall. In the morning, Dietrich wants to carry the wounded man away, but the holy fool stubbornly urges him to fetch water and pulls him toward the well. After the battle, Dietrich finds Salvation beside the well with his hands in the water. He rejo
sudya-enkhal: Don Enhal is a first-level judge and Beatriz’s father. He never appears in person in the novel: his daughter and the letters he exchanges with Alvaro provide the account of him. Beatriz’s father (ch. 9–11) In ch. 9, it emerges that Beatriz lives with her father, a first-level judge. In ch. 11, to rid himself of his persistent pupil, Alvaro writes Don Enhal a letter praising his daughter as a capable writer but asking him to prevent her from associating with him because he is being followed. Beatriz reads the letter over his shoulder. The judge’s letter (ch. 20) In ch. 20, Beatriz gives Alvaro her father’s letter. Enhal apologizes for his daughter: her stubbornness and boldness, he writes, sometimes exceed the limits of prudence. He explains that Alvaro’s work has given meaning to her life and led her into the esfera of Art, and asks him to allow Beatriz to remain his pupil. He promises to remove the surveillance and asks Alvaro not to enter black lands, where his authority does not apply. If his daughter becomes unbearable, a note will suffice, and she will not be sent again. At his daughter’s request, he has also made inquiries about the green Cherrato and discovered that it belon
tot-bez-nogtej: “The One Without Nails” is the nickname Red gives a companion in his first dugout. His real name is not stated in the novel. The Dugout (ch. 8–12) In ch. 8, his nails are broken and his fingers scraped raw, as if he spent whole days clawing at a wall. When Red breaks the work gang's resistance, he twists the man's finger and punches him in the nose. In ch. 12, his thumb becomes infected. Zustand (ch. 19) Baron Landau shows Red the pit of The One Without Nails: he is on all fours, digging the earth with his bare hands, his fingers rotting. It is the first pit Red sees in the camp and one of the most horrifying.
ugo-martines: Ugo Martinez is a mustachioed chauffeur who becomes an accidental victim of Alvaro and Fernan's suspicions. A Night at the Inn (ch. 11) While returning from Ortiyar , Fernan convinces Alvaro that a green steam carriage is following them. At night, the friends go down to the inn's lobby, and Alvaro grabs the mustachioed chauffeur by the collar. The man introduces himself as Ugo Martinez and has no idea what is happening. Two children run into the lobby, shower the friends with rice, and shout “Happiness and freedom!”: Martinez divorced his wife today and is celebrating with his children and his sister, Aunt Nelly. He explains that they have been enjoying themselves in Laerta and are now returning, that they have not been to Ortiyar, and that the green bracelet on his wrist confirms his profession as a chauffeur. The embarrassed friends apologize under a hail of rice “canister.” Consequences Alvaro is angry with himself for yielding to Fernan's suspicions, but immediately sees a plot device in what happened: Beatriz did not witness his humiliation. In the morning, he spots a green Cherrato 3-5 in the inn's courtyard and concludes that he has found the spy. He deliberately proposes to
varkhajt: Friedrich von Wahrheit is a Dangarian count and newspaper magnate. He owns four newspapers, including Glory, also called Glory of the Empire in the text. Baroness Elsa introduces him to her guests as “His Majesty's companion” and “the voice of the imperial court.” The Baroness's Reception (ch. 14) At the fishing party at Baroness Walbrecht's , the count sits at the festive table and, unlike Joriksen, enjoys flattery: when Elsa praises Glory, he nods as though urging her to continue. The baroness recounts how she once cited his newspaper in a conversation with the Kaiser, and the sovereign immediately agreed. When a dragoon cornet refuses to drink with an Ollandian prince, the count endorses their hostess's statement that there are no enemies at her table. He then approves Dietrich's toast, and at these moments the narrator calls him “the Kaiser's voice,” the man with the best knowledge of the sovereign's thoughts. That evening, the count holds the bank in a thousand-mark game of Stoss. When the players ask him about Dunkwald , he answers with a question: “Did you read about it in my Glory?”—then adds that in that case it is true: the newspaper does not print nonsense. Glory of the
viglaf: Wiglaf is Master Fritjof Joriksen's assistant and appears only in Chapter 14. He is an enormous man with thick sideburns, wearing a sleeveless top, with a blue anchor tattoo on his right shoulder. He dresses and speaks like a sailor. Appearance Wiglaf stands on the stage behind the schönbrun , his arms crossed over his chest. Master and assistant bow to the well in the same way. Assistant at the Fishing Party (ch. 14) At the fishing party at Baroness Walbrecht's , Wiglaf moves through the rows of spectators, handing out slips of paper and pencils so everyone can write down the “heartache” they want to be rid of. He then collects the slips and presents them to Joriksen on a tray. Using the sea reckoning, Joriksen checks the date, time, and weather with Wiglaf, who answers as one should aboard a ship. The assistant is not mentioned again; Joriksen's secretary Otto accompanies him on the journey to Ollandia.
vinsente-ramires: Vincente Ramires da Rimini is a master of law, a solitary man with a pointed beard and sharp mustache. In the first chapter, he sits in an expensive restaurant near the Grand Opera, notices Alvaro and his friends at the next table, and remarks that the establishment is for the higher ranks of Art and Law, yet the maestro has brought two obreros . This remark sparks the dueling debate described in detail in “The Dueling Debate with Ramires” . The restaurant (ch. 1) Ramires responds to an insult with “wisdom”: one equals seven; by bringing two obreros, Alvaro has brought “two-sevenths of a person,” as though a dismembered corpse. Alvaro challenges him to a revolver duel, but Ramires refuses: native Catalians are people of the word and settle conflicts with words. He proposes a dueling debate . Alvaro offers a stake of a thousand escudos, while Ramires asks for “a month’s income.” He wears a bracelet with a black snake, from which Alvaro deduces that his opponent serves Fatima the allen . The debate in the Chamber of the Word (ch. 1) The following day in the Chamber of the Word , Ramires unexpectedly agrees with everything his opponent says: he admits that he was angry the day before
vtoroj-ubijtsa: The Second Killer accompanies Salvador in the events of ch. 34; for the night in the castle, see “The Night at Last Winter” . The night in the castle (ch. 34) He fires from the top of the watchtower with a bolt-action rifle, a military invention that, according to Alvaro, cannot be bought in a shop. He kills one of Deserey’s agents, seriously wounds another, and shoots Fernan in the leg. In the castle hall, he stands by while Salvador interrogates the prisoners. In the cellar, as Salvador burns, the second killer throws a grenade down the stairs; the blast stuns everyone. Alvaro fires at his silhouette and wounds him in the arm and leg. When Fatima and Frey enter the cellar, the killer is tied up and taken away with the corpses. The novel does not say what happens to him afterward.
yakka: Yakka is a hunter serving Fischmeister Fritjof Joriksen . He is the first person Red meets in Dangar and one of the few to remain beside him throughout his forced labor: he guards the pit, carries water, takes him to his “prize,” and once brings the fugitive back alive from the winter forest. He is neither slave nor officer, speaks only Dangarian, and develops a strange friendship with Red, ended by killings rather than a quarrel. Character and Appearance Red first sees Yakka as an escort with narrow eyes and a flat, round face, wearing a fox-fur cap and a reindeer-hide coat. He smokes a long-stemmed pipe, carries a silver-trimmed double-barreled flintlock gun, and softly draws out the last sound of Red's name: “Reda.” This form—“Reda, grabt” (“Red, dig”)—becomes his habitual refrain. Yakka is unflappable and seldom raises his voice. He is an accurate shot—in ch. 8, he shoots a cone off a stump from about twenty paces—but does not fire without need or orders; he laughs at threats and calmly turns his back on Red. He enjoys chatting in his own language and carving wood. He believes in ancestral spirits and in the “soul” of his gun, named Eikha: a spell upon it prevents its bullet fr
zejdvist: Claus von Zeidvist is the staff captain commanding the battery to which Lieutenant Dietrich von Dort belongs. Chapter 2 opens with Zeidvist's letter to Colonel Walter Gerlach assessing Dietrich; soon afterward, the staff captain dies, and his death remains one of the acts that torments Dietrich most. Character (ch. 2) Zeidvist is abrupt and irritable. Dietrich suspects the battery may have been left in the rear because of its commander's fondness for schnapps. In his letter, Zeidvist describes the twenty-three-year-old lieutenant as unprepossessing, soft, disinclined to duel, too lenient with his orderly Milosh , and given to saying “umm” and “yes?..”; he has no inclination to promote Dietrich. Zeidvist is rude to his subordinates. Through his adjutant, he orders Dietrich to inspect the fusilier platoon and bring water—the staff captain wants to wash—and when the lieutenant returns empty-handed, he unleashes a tirade and orders him to bring ten buckets personally the next morning. Death (ch. 2–6) When an Ollandian squadron emerges from the forest at dawn, an enraged Zeidvist threatens Dietrich with a court-martial and penal servitude. Dietrich whispers to him, “I am afraid you will
zolotoj-dukat: Golden Ducat is the quartermaster at Carlos el Niña’s fort, a man with a gold tooth who addresses people as “you devil.” Meeting in a tavern (ch. 13) Alvaro, having written a despairing letter to Filippe rejecting the commission, meets Ducat in a tavern. Ducat passes on the captain’s message: he is waiting for the book and will kill Alvaro if he dies before finishing it. At the fort (ch. 18) When Alvaro comes to inquire about Juanes’s death, the sentry calls Ducat. He takes the writer to the tower and whispers, “Try, do something, go easy on him.” Later, he joins the drinking in the study. Ducat remembers about forty foreigners — Muari, Merganans, and islanders — who sailed under el Niña’s flag, and insists that none of them ever shed blood beyond a white post: a foreigner would be the first suspect, and the punishment for a white-land murder is terrible, which he illustrates with gestures. “There are no white-land murderers,” he says. He knows nothing about da Vira, although he has served for years.
aj-khinar: Ai-Khinar is one of the Ancients , described in the novel as the most fearsome. He figures in the story as a city symbol and a detail in an exhibition, rather than as a character. The statue in the Old Port (ch. 7, 18) The statue of Ai-Khinar is the symbol of Laerta’s Old Port district. It depicts a gigantic serpent rising out of the waves and spreading its wings, ready to soar into the air. Its jaws are open, and venom drips from its enormous fangs. Some joker has placed a real human skull between its jaws (ch. 7). In chapter 18, when Alvaro visits Carlos el Niña, the skull has been replaced by an empty bottle. The district beyond the black pillar where Ai-Khinar stands belongs to pirates and smugglers: here, anyone wearing a pirate’s or assassin’s bracelet may kill anyone without punishment (ch. 7). Ai-Khinar in painting (ch. 16, 32) At the “Philosophy of Horror” exhibition, Ai-Khinar is depicted as a madman. Filippe di Berro mentions him as they move between paintings, then immediately turns to a story about van Halm (ch. 16). In van Halm’s study in the castle above Tres Molinos , a portrait of Ai-Khinar hangs alongside the Shipbreaker and the Mother-and-Father (ch. 32).
alessina: Alessina is the mirna of art. Members of the esferas associated with creativity invoke her at every opportunity: Alvaro da Silva calls upon her in moments of inspiration and swears by her. She does not act in person in the novel: people speak of her, refer to her, and paint her. Symbols and invocations Her symbol is a theatrical mask. In a painting at the “Philosophy of Horror” exhibition, Alessina wears a mask, while Iolanta has a feather in her hair (ch. 16). A greeting at the faculty of literature: Dean Farmiga wishes that “Alessina may light his way” when addressing Alvaro (ch. 3). Alvaro also uses this formula himself. Oaths: Fernan, threatened with execution by firing squad in Carlos el Niña’s den, swears by Alessina that he has not yet written anything (ch. 7). Alvaro swears by her at the autopsy (ch. 24). The narrator calls Alvaro “Alessina’s favorite” and a “servant” of Iolanta as he walks in the company of an alguacil (ch. 13). The expression is also used more generally: “the servants of Iolanta and Alessina” are the esferas of Law and Art (ch. 26). Alessina Bay (ch. 7) The first section of Laerta’s waterfront is called Alessina Bay. Dons’ yachts, passenger ships, and fas
algvasily: Alguacils are Catalian keepers of order from the esfera of Law. The narrator explains in ch. 13: “Two kinds of people keep order in Catalia: guards and alguacils.” Guards and alguacils (ch. 13) The two services work together, but are organized differently. Guards belong to the esfera of Shadow . They wear thick beards but shave their mustaches to make their jaws look “heavy as a bulldog’s”; they do not wear hats, and tie their hair with red scarves in pirate fashion. They carry all sorts of weapons: clubs, parrying daggers, guns, and pistols. Guards intervene when there is no doubt that a crime has been committed: a fight somewhere fighting is forbidden, violence against a woman without a prostitute’s bracelet, or a Shadow master exceeding the authority of his guild. Alguacils belong to the esfera of Law. They take on a case when it is necessary to determine how far the letter of the Scroll has been violated, who is responsible—and whether there was a crime at all. They carry the latest weapons, carbines and revolvers, but regard their minds as their chief weapon. They wear pointed beards and mustaches “that give the face a look of haughty cunning,” and decorate their hats with a w
alleny: Allen is the highest position within an esfera: a representative of its interests at the High Table . Each of the eleven esferas has exactly three allens regardless of its population, which is why the allens of the Three Bulls are considered disadvantaged compared with those of the smaller esferas (ch. 1, 7). What is known about allens (ch. 3–34) Prim-allen. In the novel, this is the title of an esfera’s leading allen: Filippe di Berro is prim-allen of Art (ch. 3), and Fatima Ir-Reya is prim-allen of Law (ch. 28). Her bracelet is white gold with a diamond feather of the mirna Iolanta . Chapter 22 also mentions the prim-allens of Law and Shadow, whom Carlos el Niña knows. Influence. Fatima, for example, oversees the legal professionals of Law whom the factory owners hire; Mor believes that for the Reformists to win, they must persuade Fatima to forbid her lawyers from representing the factory owners (ch. 20). General Deserey addresses her as “ma donna,” a formula used when requesting a great favor (ch. 28). Vulnerability. Each year, the Table expels its worst allen. Filippe has held his place for six years (ch. 3); Fatima fears that she will not be spared during the purge (ch. 28).
belaya-zemlya: Catalian territory is divided into three kinds of land according to the crimes tolerated there. This division is connected with the esfera of Shadow and established by tradition: criminals live openly in Catalia, but they follow rules. White land (ch. 5–24) White land is a district where there is no crime at all. White pillars stand at every intersection, and a Catalian accustomed to seeing them feels safe. Here there are no bars on windows or locks on doors, no need for guards or alguacils; children play unsupervised, goods lie unprotected, and young women walk around in provocative dresses ( Alvaro notices all this in ch. 5, almost forgetting where he is). Holding someone against their will on white land is a crime, which enables Alvaro to leave Maduro’s guardroom with a revolver in his holster (ch. 13). The neighborhood where Alvaro lives, on Foucault Street, is also white, so his home has no lock. The chief taboo of white land is murder. Killing on white land is criminal in a profound, almost sacred sense: the killer is effectively spitting in the First Judge’s face, and the punishment is monstrous (ch. 9). The First Judge’s laws take intent into account: if a death is caused u
braslet: A bracelet is the chief visible indication of a Catalian’s status. It shows the esfera to which a person belongs ( Esferas ) and their rank within it. A person’s profession can be read from their bracelet; some bracelets, such as those of pirates and assassins, grant the right to do things that would be crimes for anyone else. Someone may wear several bracelets: in ch. 5, the speaker in the tavern has three—a wedding bracelet, a friendship bracelet, and the bracelet of an obrero of Craft. What is known about bracelets (ch. 0–22) The silver bracelet of a maestro. The writer Alvaro da Silva wears one on his left wrist: he is a maestro of Art. By the age of thirty-five, he hopes to exchange it for a gold one after gaining fame for a masterpiece (ch. 0). The gold bracelet of a don. A don is the head of an esfera or of a rank within it. A gold bracelet is not inherited: a don’s son receives money and knowledge from his father, but not the title (ch. 7). White gold with a diamond feather. The bracelet of the prim-allen of Law: the feather is the symbol of the mirna Iolanta , patroness of law (ch. 28). Fatima’s lawyers wear bracelets with a black snake (ch. 1). Black and yellow: the brace
darredzho: Darreggio is the mirn —the masculine form—of mechanics, or, as the exhibition puts it, engineering. He is the patron of mechanics, in keeping with the location of his temple in the craftsmen’s square. On the academy clock (ch. 5) On the tower of the Academy of Arts , Darreggio’s figurine emerges beneath an enameled sun at three in the afternoon, replacing Vinsenya . The narrator ironically calls him a lazy fellow. Darreggio in a painting (ch. 16) At the “Philosophy of Horror” exhibition in the Eliste Gallery , one painting shows Darreggio cutting open his own belly and inserting a miniature steam engine. His extracted intestines lie beside him, with flies circling above them. The caption reads: “The highest power is power over oneself.” Filippe di Berro advises Alvaro to think about it. The temple in Craftsmen’s Square (ch. 30) A grey-stone temple of Darreggio stands at the center of Laerta’s Craftsmen’s Square. It forces the flow of people around the edges of the square. Two-story houses crowd its perimeter, each containing a workshop or shop: a shoemaker’s, a hardware shop, or a coppersmith’s. The narrator says that the square recalls a time when the city was sustained by small f
dengi: In “Traces on the Water,” numbers always play a role in the story. Catalians reckon in escudos and Dangarians in marks, and a sum of money often sets events in motion. The best-known example is the seven thousand escudos that Alvaro da Silva loses in a debate. Units and means of payment The escudo is Catalia’s principal currency. Large stakes are specified as “in gold”—“a thousand escudos in gold”—while banknotes circulate in everyday life. Pesetas and pesos. Small change: in ch. 3, the narrator speaks of “the last few pesetas wrapped in a rag,” while Alvaro and Fernan complain that they do not have “a peso” in their pockets. The text does not explain the relationship between the peseta, peso, and escudo. Promissory notes and IOUs. A debtor has the right to issue a promissory note, but it is not accepted everywhere: innkeepers are happy to put a debt on a tab, but the postal service does not accept IOUs (ch. 13). The bank maintains personal accounts. Collateral in the Scroll. According to the records of the Great Scroll , any voluntary transaction is legal: rumors, seawater, and even a body part have been used as collateral (ch. 20). The mark is the principal currency of Dangar . T
drevnie: The Ancients , also called the Lords of the Abyss , are the gods of Catalia’s old religion. They live in the sea, and Catalians invoke them at every surprise or misfortune. In the novel, they are part of language and culture rather than active characters: “Oh, Ancients!”, “for the abyss’s sake,” “may the Crab devour me.” Humanity is called “the proud creation of the Ancients” in the very first scene, when Alvaro debates human equality in the Chamber of the Word (ch. 1). How Catalians speak of the Ancients Oaths and curses. “In the name of the Ancients,” “Ancients save us,” “glory to the Ancients,” “lords of the abyss,” “for the abyss’s sake,” and “may the Crab devour me” occur in the speech of Alvaro, Fernan, Lucille, Red, and other characters (ch. 4, 8, 11, 13, 15). Earlier names. The audience at the Grand Opera argues about a new production of “Señorita Violet”: supposedly, in that period the Ancients were called the Winged Ones or the Lords of the Abyss, rather than the Ancients (ch. 3). Parting curses. Carlos el Niña’s quartermaster, Golden Ducat , passes on the captain’s words: if the writer dies before finishing the book, Carlos will “make an arrangement with the Ancients,” d
duelnyj-spor: The dueling debate is the central institution of Catalian law. Everyone, according to the First Judge’s code, may defend their rights through debate. Catalians call themselves people of the word: conflicts that other peoples settle with bullets are brought to the Chamber of the Word. Any question—from the position of a fence between fields to the foundations of the state—may be challenged; only what has been proved in a fair debate is considered correct. How a debate works (ch. 1, 22) Under the First Judge’s code, a debate requires: an arbiter with a bracelet of the esfera of Law, who takes an oath with a hand on the code; duelists or their substitutes; at least five jurors . They must either know neither of the two debaters or know both equally well. Jurors are unpaid and attend for the spectacle: the Chamber of the Word is called a free theater. The procedure is as follows: the secretary records the opponent’s name; the bailiff summons the jurors; a small weather vane determines who speaks first. The winner is the person whose arguments persuade the jurors. The aim is to convince the jurors, not to change the opponent’s mind; victory is recorded on the Scroll and becomes truth un
ejkha: Eikha is the gun belonging to Yakka , a hunter and assistant to Master Joriksen . To Yakka, she is more than a weapon: he believes that Eikha has a soul, and he talks to her. eliga: Eliga is the mirna of luck. In popular belief, she has two faces: one womanly and kind, the other a serpent’s. If she smiles, good luck follows; if she shows her serpent face, disaster strikes. Catalians invoke her in gambling and in any other situation where everything depends on chance. Her image (ch. 4) Red describes Eliga in terms of luck, “odd or even,” heads or tails. A beautiful woman sitting astride a cannon is tattooed on his forearm. Her womanly face is smiling, while the serpent’s face hides beneath a mass of hair, with only an eye and its vertical pupil visible. Three are enormous: Craft, later called the esfera of Production, Agriculture, and Service. Politics rests on the esferas: at the High Table , each is represented by three allens , no more and no less, so the Three Bulls hold nine of the thirty-three seats, while the eight smaller esferas hold twenty-four. This dictionary collects words that occur in the text and may be unfamiliar to the reader. Each definition is based on the book; where a concept has its own article, a link is provided. kolodets: Wells are the central mystery of the world in which the novel takes place. These are not ordinary water wells: in a true Well, instead of a bottom there is mist and another world inhabited by monsters. Following the author’s working name, the entire series about this world is called the “World of Wells.” The novel’s three storylines—those of the Catalian Red , the Dangarian Dietrich von Dort , and the writer Alvaro da Silva —converge around wells of different kinds. sinkho: Sinkho is a Catalian mourning custom. When someone in a household dies, a small dry sinkho tree in a pot is placed on the porch. The narrator calls it “a symbol of the recent death that has visited the house.” Ribbons (ch. 5) Traditionally, anyone may tie a blue, red, or black ribbon to a branch as a sign of their attitude toward the deceased. The novel explicitly says only that the colors convey that attitude. Context makes clear that blue ribbons express kind words about the dead: on Dr. Garcia Juanes’s tree, all the ribbons are blue, and Alvaro and Fernan have never seen such a thing before. No one wished to say a single bad word about the doctor. Juanes’s widow says that her husband “went into the blue beyond,” an expression for death. The meanings of the red and black ribbons are not explained in the text. This observation about the ribbons plays a part in Alvaro’s first theory: if the doctor had no enemies, why kill him?

svitok: The Great Scroll is the central repository of records in Catalia . Every Catalian hopes to leave a mark upon it: the writer Alvaro da Silva dreams of inscribing his name on the Scroll as his grandfather Ricardo Flores , author of “The Snake in the Reeds,” once did. The names of the heroes of Solanta are entered on the Scroll as the names of heroes (ch. 3). What is entered on the Scroll (ch. 22) The Scroll records not the population but Truth: whatever has prevailed in a debate before jurors ( Dueling Debate ). If a publisher and a critic debate whether a novel is a masterpiece, and the jurors rule that it is, an entry appears on the Scroll and acquires the force of law: the author’s heirs gain the right to demand reprints, and teachers may assign it to students. Personal truths are entered in the same way: the award of bracelets and titles, the defense of examination work, marriages and divorces, adoption, crimes, honors and their forfeiture, the question of who should pay to bury an unloved relative, and much more (ch. 22). Organization (ch. 1–24) The Table seats allens : three from each of the eleven esferas , no more and no less, for a total of thirty-three seats. The three large esferas, the “Three Bulls” ( Three Bulls ), therefore occupy nine seats, while the eight smaller ones occupy twenty-four. They want reform based on proportional representation. The Table’s authority is limited. In accordance with the proverb “A tree grows on its own roots,” it handles only the foreign policy of Catalia as a whole and relations between esferas; the dons settle their esferas’ internal affairs. Decisions are made by voting. The Table is headed by the supreme allen, or supremo; in ch. 22 and 24, an election scheduled for roughly six months later is discussed, but the novel does not describe the electoral procedure. Pur

He adds poverty to his list of a hero’s attributes: a rich man inspires envy, a needy man is relatable to the reader, and a well-fed man wants nothing. The student in the front row with a golden fountain pen— Beatriz —argues with him, while a yellow-haired Reformist student ( Wasp ) thanks him for his speech in the Chamber of the Word. Alvaro goes to the dean of the faculty of letters, Don Farmiga , to ask for an advance, but is refused: he drank away the previous advance and still owes five lectures. The dean threatens to replace him with the poet Cecilia Armani. In chapter 13, the series ends with a lecture on a hero’s flaws, which Alvaro delivers listlessly and without preparation.
