bargot: Bargot is the capital of Ollandia (ch. 31). It stands in the south of the country, on the navigable River Khursla , surrounded by wealthy principalities; this is the part of the country the Dangarian strategists covet most. On the author’s map, Bargot is labeled on the river’s southern bank, south of the red arrow marking Kurtzleben’s army. The threat (ch. 31) General of Infantry Kurtzleben, “a merciless butcher with an iron will,” leads the strongest of the three Dangarian armies southward. By chapter 31, he has yet to succeed: river supply arrangements have failed, and the Ollandians have fortified the southern bank and brought up mortars. Field Marshal Reiniger gives him sixty days to cross the Khursla and besiege Bargot, but forbids a frontal assault: four of Hofmeyer’s divisions are to strike the flank as part of an outflanking maneuver. The novel does not reveal how the siege ends.
brega: Brega is the industrial center of Catalia . The author’s map labels it “Province of Brega—the industrial center of Catalia.” It has the largest coal deposits, and the broad River Monho serves as a transport artery. The novel says that Brega has more smokestacks than a forest has trees, and that when it rains, the drops turn black (ch. 20). A traveler’s view (ch. 4) A traveler taking the train from Laerta spends another full day in Brega after Selezia . Following the River Monho, sometimes approaching it and sometimes drawing away, the train passes towns packed close together, each bristling with rows of factory chimneys. Workshop sirens answer locomotive whistles, steamships and barges scurry along the river, and the carriage windows become coated in soot. Beyond Brega begins the Kabarda steppe. Industry and Esperanza (ch. 7–20) Brega supplies the steam-powered machines that displace workers in Laerta (ch. 11), as well as compact engines; saltpeter for Brega’s cannon is imported from Muaris (ch. 17). Ten years earlier, Brega suffered the same unemployment crisis now beginning in Laerta. The engineer Mor , inventor of the pressure condenser, organized the dismissed workers, who chal
chinkhar: Chinkhar is a northern land that Dangar conquered in the past and that now answers to the Kaiser. On the author’s map, its name is written in italics among the mountains in the northwestern part of Dangarian territory. History (ch. 10) Seventy years ago, during the Chinkhar Wars, Empress Augusta looked after officers’ widows. But the war dragged on, producing widows faster than houses could be built, and the empress eventually made peace. She never started another war. The conquest of Chinkhar was completed only thirty years later, under her grandson. The capital’s Witwen district preserves the memory of those wars ( Hofstadt ). The Chinkharians (ch. 14, 27) In chapter 14, the narrator identifies an aquiline nose, sharply defined cheekbones, and intent green eyes as distinctive features of a Chinkharian northerner—features like Joriksen’s . Three generations ago, people like him “gave people like von Dort a hard time,” but then they accepted the Kaiser’s rule, moved to the capital, and became fishermen. Chapter 27 says that Fischmeister Fritjof has “some Chinkharian blood,” which is considered a blemish in his ancestry: this is precisely why he was sent to serve in Dunkwald . In an
dunkvald: Dunkwald is a settlement deep within Dangar , concealed by thick forest. According to the account in chapter 27, it is inhabited by hundreds of stones belonging to the Fishermen’s Guild, all of whom do nothing but dig wells. They try different methods, conditions, and Zustands ( Zustand ), while apprentices record every attempt in ledgers. When water appears at the bottom, a fischmeister looks into it and gives his verdict, after which the well is filled in. In half a century, not one of these wells has become a schönbrun . The settlement (ch. 23, 27) Dunkwald contains the women’s settlement of Katzen (its name is a joke), barracks, a temple of the Spiritual Sower, the administration’s mansion, dugouts, and a work clearing; the only road passable to vehicles leads to the town and the railway. When the settlement was founded half a century ago, it was taken seriously: the best masters came to test their theories, and the Kaiser sent agents. Now the unluckiest and lowest-born are posted here: Fischmeister Fritjof and the Kaiser’s Claw Wolf were assigned ten-year postings. Baron Landau runs the settlement, with its guards and foremen under his authority. Red in Dunkwald (ch. 23–33) In
ejring: Eyring is a city in Dangar named after the family that owns it. On the author’s map, a note beside it reads “the ancestral seat of those very von Eyrings”—a reference to chapter 17, where Dietrich , learning that his cover story makes him Katrina von Eyring’s cousin, asks whether these are the Eyrings after whom the city is named. “The city is their hereditary possession,” Olkha replies. The von Eyring family (ch. 17, 25, 29, 31) The Eyrings are an ancient and powerful family. Prince Lenz is told that killing Lieutenant von Eyring over a trivial matter would earn him influential enemies at court, especially if the killer were a foreigner (ch. 25). In their cover story, Dietrich and Katrina are cousins from a cadet branch of the family. Its head is Margrave Maximian von Eyring, a miser who nonetheless protects his own (ch. 29); in chapter 31, the calling cards of Count Ludwig von Lurd and Margrave von Eyring help secure Dietrich’s release from the gendarmerie. The city itself is not described in the text.
galereya-eliste: The Eliste Gallery is one of the landmarks of Laerta . Marble statues of the mirnas stand on its roof, turning pink at sunset: this is the very image that opens Alvaro’s evening walk in the preface. The collection The gallery is famous for its three-hundred-year-old collection: faded icons from the previous millennium, resembling children’s drawings with patches of gilding; battle panoramas from the feudal era (“The Battle of Lamertina,” “The Conquest of Brega,” “The Death of King Augustus the Pale”); portraits by Velanyes, with stiff poses but lifelike faces; and engravings by Emil Flare. Scandalous works are shown on the temporary-exhibitions floor. The “Philosophy of Horror” exhibition (ch. 16, 18) In chapter 16, the gallery hosts “Philosophy of Horror: An Artist’s View of the Myths of the Ancients.” Don Filippe invites Alvaro and takes him from canvas to canvas: Iolanta and Alessina argue about art, Darreggio inserts a small steam engine into his belly, Ikhtrodan the Shipbreaker is coiled into a ring like a serpent, and the mirna of luck, Eliga , is shown with a bullet hole in her temple. The exhibition shares its title with van Halm’s unfinished book ( Philosophy of Horror ).
gerona: Gerona is a city in Catalia. On the author’s map It is labeled on the author’s world map in northern Catalia, beside the fortress of Indra and south of the border with Ollandia . The name does not occur in the first book’s text, so neither its role nor its population is known. The nearest described stretches of the journey are Kabarda—a land known for its stubborn men, quarrelsome bulls, and bickering women—and the border fortress of Indra (ch. 4), through which the railway from Laerta to Ollandia passes.
ginarva: Ginarva is a town on the River Khursla in Ollandia . In chapter 4, its name is written “Girnava”; on the author’s map, it is “Ginarva.” The end of the tracks (ch. 4) The reader traveling from Catalia reaches the end of the rails here. The only way to continue is to board a low-sided steamship that takes three days to make its way down the Khursla, greeted at every landing by a brass band. At a bend in the river stands a border bastion, which fires a farewell cannon shot; the steamer answers with its whistle. Beyond lies Mergana (ch. 4).
grand-opera: The Grand Opera is a theater in the center of Laerta . In the preface, the narrator observes that on the evening the story begins, a line for tickets stretches from its steps: the posters advertise “Señorita Violet,” featuring the celebrated Don Filippe , making his first stage appearance in a year. “Señorita Violet” (ch. 1, 3) In chapter 3, Alvaro watches the performance from a box to which Filippe’s Muari servant has invited him. The plot runs as follows: the hidalgo Don Laurent loves blue-eyed Violet but seduces women of ever higher rank; the queen exiles Violet to an island, where she marries a kindly sailor; Laurent then returns with pleas, and in the classic version Violet stabs herself. Don Filippe, who sings Laurent’s part, demanded a rewritten ending: Violet takes a double-barreled pistol, it misfires twice, and she falls into Laurent’s arms. During the interval, the audience debates the ending in the refreshment rooms; most approve of the moral that dying for love is the last thing anyone should do. After the performance, Filippe, without his makeup, receives Alvaro backstage and commissions a book about his friends, the heroes of a famous exploit (see The Solantan Expedi
indra: Indra is a Catalian border fortress on the railway route to Ollandia . In the text (ch. 4) In chapter 4, where the reader travels by train from Laerta , it is mentioned as the last stop: a town “compressed by a ring of fortifications like a maiden’s bosom by a corset.” An officer checks the passenger’s papers and wishes them a speedy return to Catalia, while Indra sees the train off with pennants waving from its bastions. Beyond Indra begins a belt of marshes, with the land of the Ollandians on the far side. On the author’s map On the author’s map, Indra is labeled in the northern part of the blue region, north of Brega and beside the city of Gerona. There are no other mentions in the text.
khofshtadt: Hofstadt is the capital of Dangar , “Mighty Hofstadt,” as the narrator calls it in chapter 10. It stands on the River Wunde, which swells to a width of half a verst in spring and teems with barges and steamships, but shrinks to almost a stream by late summer. Once a year, for roughly a month, the river disappears entirely. This month is called Gehai , meaning “sacred”: people say that the Sower’s tears fill the Wunde, and when it dries up, the god is happy. On the author’s map, an arrow beside Hofstadt bears the note “And this is where Dietrich returned to his wife.” The city’s layout (ch. 10) The river runs from north to south, forming an elbow within the city. On the western bank, inside the bend, lies the Schlissel district—the “key to power over the empire.” Here stand ten ministries, the general staff headquarters, the patriarchal cathedral, the treasury, the treasure house, the Life Guards’ barracks, the cadet school, and the star-shaped imperial palace with its ten towers. Six bridges fan out from Schlissel across the Wunde, connecting the center with the districts on the left bank. The city has docks, a railway bridge, and Widows’ Square; the poor travel in human-drawn carr
khursla: The Khursla is a navigable river on which stand Ginarva , Bargot , and the capital of Mergana . It is labeled in light blue on the author’s map, with its western continuation shown as a dotted line extending beyond the depicted land. The river journey (ch. 4) From Ginarva, the reader travels downstream for three days aboard a low-sided steamship. Bands stand at every landing, and a border bastion overlooks a bend in the river. Beyond Ollandia, the river runs through Mergana, where the traveler goes ashore at the Professors’ Bridge. Farther on, it reaches the Kobold Sea, where a Dangarian port has strict inspections and coastal forts. A wartime barrier (ch. 31) The Dangarian command planned to supply its southern army by steamship, via the sea and the Khursla. At the beginning of summer, Kurtzleben brought his troops to the river, but the steamships failed to arrive: part of the route crossed Mergana’s territory, and Mergana refused the vessels passage. The foreign ministry resolved the issue, but the ships had already been reassigned to other routes. Now the army must cross the river through an outflanking maneuver carried out by Hofmeyer , rather than a frontal assault.
klinika-miloserdiya: Mercy Clinic is a hospital for the mentally ill in Catalia . The clinic is important to the novel because the philosopher Liess van Halm , a witness to the secret of the five heroes of Solanta, is confined there. The journal entry (ch. 24) The butler Emil is the first to mention the clinic. Returning from a nighttime call, Dr. Juanes wrote in his journal: “Liess van Halm, 49. Prelim. diag.: schizophrenia. Transferred to Mercy Clinic.” When Beatriz asks where the philosopher is now, Emil replies: “At Mercy Clinic, unless they’ve moved him. Or perhaps he’s dead.” Beatriz suggests that the doctor “packed him off to a madhouse” to silence him. The visit (ch. 26) Alvaro and Beatriz come to the clinic to see van Halm. Miguel, an orderly wearing a sleeveless white coat, demands twenty escudos for a visit: “That is the set price. Everyone pays it.” Alvaro argues that, as a free man of the word, he has the right to speak to another man of the word without charge, but Beatriz pays anyway. The narrator explains the practice: Catalians are prepared to pay only for results, and a stay in a hospital does not restore reason. laerta: Laerta is the capital of Catalia and the principal setting of Traces on the Water. Alvaro da Silva’s story begins and ends here; the convict Red also longs to return to Laerta, his hometown. Location Laerta stands on the southern coast, in the part of the country known as Beautiful Catalia: a land of warm weather, theaters, universities, and architectural gems. In the Dangarian generals’ assessment, the sea belongs to Laerta. On the author’s map, Laerta is labeled at the very south of the blue region, with a dotted route arrow leading away from it and marked “Beginning of the Solantan Expedition’s Voyage”; to the northwest, the map shows Ortiyar Fortress, guarding the approaches to the city. The city’s layout The city is divided into eleven districts, one for each esfera. The districts have their own emblems: a slipper for Service, a cogwheel for Craft, and a bull’s head for Agriculture. Districts are colored according to the rules of the “lands”: in white areas, such as the Arts district, there are no locks or guards and murder is virtually impossible; grey areas, such as the Craft district and the meeting point of districts near the Three Bulls tavern, permit theft and fighting b
latsen: Latsen is a city in the center of Ollandia , on the Plyutva–Latsen–Mershants railway line. On the author’s map, three red arrows fan out from it: Kurtzleben’s army heads south, Brojenstoff’s north, and Hofmeyer’s southeast. The broadest arrow points toward Latsen from the western border, marking the invasion’s general direction, while a nearby black arrow is labeled “This is where Dietrich won the battle.” Occupation (ch. 6) The Dangarians captured the city roughly three months before chapter 6. The square is clean and a brass band plays, but there are almost no listeners, and only women wait for water at the fountain. Here Dietrich meets Olkha , while Major Klein of the Kaiser’s Claws receives him in the town hall. Headquarters (ch. 25, 28, 31) In chapter 31, Latsen is described as the country’s geographical center, whose capture split it into north and south. Field Marshal Reiniger has installed himself in the former assembly hall of the Latsen Voivodeship’s nobility; the generals’ conference also takes place here. In chapter 28, the Catalian general Deserey reports that the Plyutva–Latsen–Mershants railway is under construction, and that Kurtzleben’s and Brojenstoff’s armies are
mershants: Mershants is an Ollandian fortress in the east of the country, near the Catalian border, and the center of the voivodeship known as Mershants. On the author’s map, it stands beside a large lake on the eastern frontier; an arrow for Hofmeyer’s army leads to it from Latsen . The siege (ch. 14, 28, 31) As early as chapter 14, we are told that Hofmeyer’s regiments are outside Mershants, that the campaign’s objective is to break through into Catalia and lay railway tracks, and that the merchants of Hofstadt are awaiting victory. In chapter 28, the Catalian general Deserey reports that Hofmeyer now has twenty-five thirty-pounder siege mortars suitable for demolishing fortresses. Chapter 31 describes the fortress in greater detail: its walls are protected by two Catalian rifled howitzers with a range of about four versts, which mow down the Dangarian batteries; to the east lies a marsh that freezes in winter. Hofmeyer proposes leading two or three hundred dismounted “eagles” across the frozen marsh to the wall in winter, blowing it up, and disabling the howitzers; Field Marshal Reiniger rejects the plan as suicidal. Major Klein hopes the general will be delayed near Latsen, in which case
ortiyar: Ortiyar is a fortress and railway junction in a narrow valley, thirty miles from Laerta . Apart from one other pass, it is the only place where the railway networks of northeastern “Mighty” Catalia and southern “Beautiful” Catalia connect: streams of freight pass through the junction before spreading across the country. There is no trading town in the valley—there was no room for one—only a transshipment station and a fortress. On the author’s map, Ortiyar is marked as “Ortiyar Fortress,” with the nearby note “General Deserey serves here.” The fortifications (ch. 9) The word “fortress” suggests high walls and drawbridges, but the narrator’s description of Ortiyar is quite different: a complex system of bastions and redoubts, scarps and counterscarps, concealed firing positions, and underground ammunition supply routes. It cannot be approached without coming under crossfire from at least three positions, and the military calls it the “shield of Laerta.” There is also a training ground: at the artillery range, Alvaro and his companions watch mortars, bombards, and canister shot being fired, try binoculars with rangefinding markings, and listen to the general explain linear and quadra
palata-slova: The Chamber of the Word is a building in Laerta where dueling debates are resolved according to the code of the First Judge . From outside, it is an “upturned bunch of grapes” without a single right angle, its “grape” halls varying in size; the text gives their number as thirty-one or thirty-seven. For more about its legal foundations, see Catalia . Procedure for a debate (ch. 1) A debate requires an arbiter wearing a bracelet of the Law esfera, two disputants, and at least five jurors who know both parties equally well or neither of them. Jurors are unpaid and attend for the spectacle: the Chamber is called a “free theater.” A little weather vane decides who speaks first. A clerk records the opponent’s name, and a bailiff summons the jurors. In chapter 1, Alvaro debates Vincente Ramires here ( The Dueling Debate with Ramires ), and the arbiter observes that the debate must not be allowed to descend into truisms. Its role in society (ch. 7–22) The Chamber of the Word settles every kind of conflict: divorce, workers’ rights, and entitlement to the title of don. The Chamber awards bracelets after an examination (ch. 12), so the verdict “the arguments are unquestionably compelling” is
plyutva: Plyutva is a city in western Ollandia , where the railway line to Latsen and Mershants begins. On the author’s map, it is labeled right beside the Dangarian border. The fall of Plyutva (ch. 2, 10) At the beginning of the novel, Plyutva has already fallen: the war has moved east, while Lieutenant Dietrich’s battery remains behind to guard the junction in the rear. Dietrich recalls praying during the siege to become an officer rather than remain a common eagle without land or stones. Later (ch. 10), we learn that Plyutva was bombarded, that “half the city was blown apart,” and that ten thousand Ollandians were branded as stones. Reports in chapter 31 describe it as “destroyed almost to its foundations.” The railway (ch. 28–31) The Plyutva–Mershants line is the only railway supplying the Dangarian army; the Catalian general Deserey learns that the line between Plyutva, Latsen, and Mershants is under construction (ch. 28). Dietrich’s first battle took place at the hundredth verst of the Plyutva–Latsen line (ch. 29). The voivodeship to which the city belongs is called the Plyutva Voivodeship.
posledniaya-zima: Last Winter is a ruined feudal castle on a plateau above Tres Molinos , known to the locals as the House Above. Alvaro da Silva gives it the name “Last Winter” in chapter 34. In chapter 32, it is simply an ominous house: a boarded-up wing, a raven on the chimney, and red ribbons marking the areas visitors may enter. The House Above (ch. 32) The Merganan recluse Liess van Halm bought the castle two years earlier. He lived in seclusion and sent out manuscripts with his servants, then suddenly dismissed them, ordered mirrors delivered, and sent out letters. A week later, guests arrived at the castle: a factory owner, a noble corsair, a grey-haired gentleman with a military bracelet, and a veiled lady—the heroes of the Solanta expedition. The factory owner later returned with a doctor. Afterward, van Halm was found insane. The townspeople are convinced the castle is cursed: before the philosopher, it belonged to Nivendey , who won an enslaved woman—the fifth wife of a Muari sultan—at dice and was arrested. Senora Marques has collected an entire catalogue of misfortunes connected with the castle. The Dangarian servants (ch. 32–34) As chapter 32 reveals, van Halm hired six new servants b
seleziya: Selezia is a province of Catalia . On the author’s map, a humorous note beside its name calls it “the land of rice fields and dreary ballads.” In chapter 4, the narrator describes it as vast seas of rice with little islands of villages and the beacons of small churches, inducing drowsiness; chapter 16 calls it “a dreary land of ruins and rice fields.” Geography and everyday life The train from Laerta heads northwest through the Darineian Range and the White Bone Pass, then crosses Selezia (ch. 4). Faramo station is built from soot-grey stone left over from a count’s castle destroyed in the Third War of Kings; one castle tower still stands, resembling a broken tooth. The plateau is cool, with snow in winter (ch. 32). One colorful detail is that Alvaro dines on paella to the sound of Selezian ballads (ch. 1)—the “Selezian ballad” is a recognized musical or song genre in the novel. Among Red’s scars is a mark left by a “Selezian dagger” (ch. 12); the text does not make clear whether this refers to the province or to the country of Seleza. Van Halm and Tres Molinos (ch. 16, 26, 32, 34) The philosopher Liess van Halm , a native of Mergana , settled in Selezia after buying an estate on t
solanta: Solanta is a small island surrounded by dangerous reefs and currents in the Miriam Sea. It is linked to Catalia by an alliance treaty signed, according to Count von Lurd , thirteen years earlier (ch. 17); the exploit discussed in the novel took place sixteen years before the story begins (ch. 3). Its heroes were Carlos el Niña , Maduro , Deserey , Fatima , Juanes , and the deceased Rodrigo da Vira . The island and the treaty (ch. 17) The island had been a Muari base ( Muari Emirates ) against Catalian pirates of the Shadow esfera. Reefs protected it, but one pirate schooner passed through them at night, captured a coastal fort, and trained its cannon on the doge’s palace. The treaty was lenient: the doge allowed Catalia to purchase brante trees—buoyant raw material suitable for airships—and permitted its fleet to enter the ports under a flag of peace. As a result, the Muari lost their supremacy over the Miriam Sea. The expedition (ch. 22, 28, 34) The story of what happened is revealed in pieces. Fatima is half-Solantan, her mother coming from the island, which is why she joined the expedition and conducted negotiations with the doge (ch. 28). Carlos bought a chart of the approach t
staryj-port: The Old Port is a district on the Laerta waterfront, identified in chapter 7 as “black”: the law permits wearers of pirate or assassin bracelets to commit almost any crime there. Posts divide the port: Alessina Bay, with the dons’ yachts; Christopher’s Port, with grey posts, where the law’s reach is limited; and the Old Port, with a black one. Murder here incurs a fine for “encroaching on someone else’s work.” For more on the rules, see White, Grey, and Black Land and The Shadow Esfera . Carlos’s fort (ch. 7) Carlos el Niña’s home is a former military bastion with cannon in the Old Port’s fort. Guards meet the “scribblers” at the entrance; in the courtyard, smuggled goods are being sorted, with a taster using thimble-sized cups, girls handling silks, and practice duels taking place. This is where Alvaro and Fernan come to find the first hero of their planned book. The attack on Alvaro (ch. 18–20) A statue of Ai-Khinar stands at the entrance to the Old Port. The district is a haven for thieves, bandits, and prostitutes, and it is here, on his way back from Carlos, that Alvaro is struck with brass knuckles before his attacker shoots through his right palm with the words “Don’t write.
tres-molinos: Tres Molinos (“Three Mills”) is a small town in a gorge in Selezia , where Alvaro da Silva and Fernan arrive in chapter 32 to investigate what happened to the philosopher van Halm . An overnight train from Laerta reaches the station, a hundred miles from Seleza; in the morning, after coffee, the passenger gets off. The town (ch. 32) The narrator ironically describes Tres Molinos as “the dullest of backwaters”: three hundred and twenty inhabitants, a town hall with a clock, running water, an inn called Comfortable Rooms, taverns called Breakfasts in Boxes and the Holy Torero, and a shop called Odds and Ends. The three windmills that gave the town its name do not grind wheat—there is none in rice-growing Selezia—but pump water into the water tower’s tank. Locals navigate by three directions: “near the temple,” meaning the temple of the Ancient Lords a mile south, closed shortly after the First Judge; “up above,” meaning the House Above, an old castle on the plateau; and “over there,” meaning everywhere else. After the temple closed, the locals say, the region stopped developing. The characters get to know the town through two guides: Javier Salam, nicknamed “Need Anything?” ( Javier
tri-byka: The Three Bulls is a tavern in Laerta , standing on grey land where the Craft, Service, and Agriculture districts meet. Three emblems appear on its walls: a slipper for Service, a cogwheel for Craft, and a bull’s head for Agriculture. The name also belongs to an informal alliance of esferas, the left wing of the High Table . A welcoming house (ch. 5, 11) In chapter 5, Alvaro , Fernan , and Lucille dine here. Regulars discuss justice and how to reshape the High Table, pronounce the word “obrero” with pride, and refer to dons and maestros as “them.” One speaker complains that moving from one esfera to another is almost impossible. Chapter 11 describes the Three Bulls as an alliance of Craft and Service opposing the factory owners. Refuge and headquarters (ch. 20, 28, 30) After escaping the Old Port , the wounded Alvaro finds friends here: the tavern keeper recognizes him, and a doctor stitches his palm (ch. 20).
